analysis.one_liner: Directs the EPA to ban discharges of plastic pellets and other pre-production plastics into U.S. waters.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 89 House cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Plastic pellets ("nurdles") — the tiny raw plastic discs melted down to make nearly all plastic products — spill from factories, trucks, trains, and ships into rivers and oceans, where fish, birds, and shellfish eat them and microplastics end up in drinking water and seafood. This bill would have ordered the EPA, within 60 days, to write rules banning the discharge of pellets and other pre-production plastic from any facility that makes, uses, packages, or transports them, and to write that ban into all water pollution permits for those facilities. It never got a hearing or a vote in the House committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who fish, swim in, and drink from U.S. waters, and coastal and Great Lakes communities whose fisheries and shorelines absorb pellet pollution. Taxpayers and utilities that currently bear cleanup costs would also benefit from stopping pellets at the source.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who fish, swim, and drink

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the EPA to issue a final rule, within 60 days of enactment, prohibiting the discharge of plastic pellets and other pre-production plastic from regulated plastics facilities and from any point source that makes, uses, packages, or transports pellets.
The prohibition would be written into all wastewater and stormwater permits and performance standards for those facilities, making it enforceable rather than voluntary.

Because pellets escape through wastewater, stormwater, and spills during transport and packaging, the bill targeted the main routes by which nurdles reach rivers, lakes, and coastal waters that people fish, swim in, and drink from.

analysis.who_pays: Plastics manufacturers and any facility that makes, uses, packages, or transports pellets, which would have had to install containment and wastewater controls to meet a zero-discharge standard. These are large, profitable industries with the resources to comply; costs to consumers would be minimal.

drawbacks.text: The bill set a 60-day deadline for the EPA to issue a final rule with no interim comment period, an unusually compressed process that would have left industry and states little time to shape how a zero-discharge requirement is implemented.

A statutory prohibition of all pellet discharges into wastewater, stormwater, and runoff is a strict standard; facilities would need to install containment and stormwater controls, and compliance costs would fall on small as well as large plastics handlers, though these costs are modest relative to typical industrial compliance burdens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — stopping a major, largely unregulated source of microplastic pollution in public waters — was real and cheap relative to its cost, since pellet-containment controls are routine equipment and housekeeping for handlers rather than a fundamental redesign of production. The strongest objection is process, not substance: dictating the specific content of an EPA rule within 60 days bypasses the agency's normal public comment process, and a rigid statutory zero-discharge rule leaves less flexibility for site-specific conditions than agency-drafted standards would. But because the bill never advanced out of committee, its design flaws were never tested; the practical result of its failure is simply that pellet pollution continues unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its water subcommittee, and was never scheduled for a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 12, 2024, with 89 cosponsors (88 Democrats and 1 Republican), and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, which is the last action recorded; no hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired, as do all bills not passed before a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastics manufacturers, shippers, and packagers that handle plastic pellets are better off: no discharge ban was enacted and pellet losses to waterways remain largely unpoliced.

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 88 Democratic cosponsors plus one Republican.

for.name: 89 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including original cosponsors such as Reps. Peltola, Huffman, Bonamici, and Raskin.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 88 of 89 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the bill was never advanced by the committee.

industries.industry: Plastic resin producers and pellet transport/packaging companies
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited any discharge of pellets from facilities that make, use, package, or transport them, forcing investment in containment and stormwater controls. Their interest ran against the public's here, since their plastic waste ends up in shared waters.
